intro: Artur Schnabel plays the third movement of the Piano Sonata No. 30, Op. 109, Gesangvoll, mit innigster Empfindung: six variations on a quiet theme in E major, with quick counterpoint and trills in both hands. The movement ends with the original sixteen bars of the theme.

sections.label: Theme · song theme in sixteen bars
sections.mNote: Two repeated halves, with a dotted rhythm in three.

sections.label: Var 1 · Melody an octave higher
sections.mNote: The right hand carries the melody above left-hand chords.

sections.label: Var 2 · The hands exchange short phrases
sections.mNote: Light exchanges alternate with a canon

sections.label: Var 3–5 · Two-part Allegro, 9/8, fugato
sections.mNote: Two-part Allegro, a slower variation in 9/8, then a fugato.

sections.label: Var 6 · Repeated Bs and trills
sections.mNote: The beat is divided into progressively smaller note values.

relations.basis: The sixteen-bar theme has two repeated eight-bar halves; both excerpts lie in its first half and repeat. relations.label: The theme’s second half repeats
relations.basis: Both excerpts lie in the second eight-bar half of the opening theme and its written repeat. relations.label: The plain theme returns
relations.basis: After the sixth variation, Beethoven restores the opening theme without the earlier variation figuration; the listening map places this return near 750 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.958, sustained 16 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 749 s (cache/form/beethoven-109-variations.txt, candidate 11; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Theme in E major
cues.text: Beethoven headed the movement Gesangvoll, mit innigster Empfindung (songfully, with the deepest feeling). The melody is in E major, and its stress falls on the second beat of the three-beat bar. The theme runs to sixteen bars, and each half is repeated.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s heading in the 1820 sonata; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 16 No. 153, printed p. 104, theme and repeat signs. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation I
cues.text: The first variation places the melody an octave higher and adds short ornaments. The left hand plays a bass note followed by a chord, in the manner of a slow dance. Beethoven marks the tune molto espressivo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 104–105, Variation I: Molto espressivo, melody an octave above the theme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Maximiliane Brentano
cues.text: The sonata is dedicated to Maximiliane Brentano. Beethoven had known her since her childhood, and in 1812 he gave the young pianist a short trio to encourage her playing. Nine years later, when he sent her this sonata, he wrote: “I see you all before me.”
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Maximiliane Brentano, Vienna, 6 December 1821; the letter and the earlier gift of Trio WoO 39 are reproduced and documented at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.

cues.title: Variation II
cues.text: Leggieramente (lightly). The hands pass short figures between them, with brief rests. In the next passage two right-hand voices imitate one another above steady left-hand quavers, and Beethoven then combines the two kinds of writing.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 105–106, Variation II; its three successive kinds of writing are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variations III to V
cues.text: The third variation is marked Allegro vivace and is in 2/4, with two fast lines. The fourth is slower, in 9/8. The fifth is a fugato in several voices, and the key stays E major throughout these changes of tempo.
cues.evidence: Variations III–V, tempo and metre headings and contrapuntal writing: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven); Giovanni Biamonti’s account at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final variation, repeated B
cues.text: The final variation returns to the theme’s slow tempo, with repeated Bs above the melody. The crotchets divide into quavers, then triplets, then shorter values. The repeated notes become trills, and the melody continues in the middle register.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 110: Tempo primo del tema, cantabile, repeated B, successive subdivisions and trills.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trills in both hands
cues.text: Long trills run through the final variation. Runs pass above them, then move into the left hand while the right hand continues to trill. The pianist must sustain a singing line within the quick notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 110–112, final variation. This cue retains the established final-variation passage time.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the theme, E major
cues.text: The trills end, and the original theme returns in E major, marked cantabile, with its plain chords and dotted rhythm. This time each half is played once, without repeats. A quiet chord closes the sonata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 112: diminuendo and pp at the end of the trills, then the theme without repeat signs and a quiet E-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A repeated B above the song
transitions.how: The fast fugato of the fifth variation closes, and Tempo primo del tema brings back the tempo of the theme. The metre changes from cut time to 3/4. The key stays E major. The piano plays the melody in slow notes, with a repeated B above it and a bass that moves once per beat. Later the repeated notes turn into trills.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 109–110; Biamonti’s account of Variations V and VI at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.

transitions.title: From the trill to the theme
transitions.how: The right-hand trill moves down into the middle of the keyboard as the left hand’s arpeggios grow quieter. Beethoven writes più dimin., then pianissimo. The trill stops, the bass holds E, and the original melody returns above it, cantabile, with its plain chords and dotted rhythm.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 112, the last systems of Variation VI and the restored theme. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
